title: Joint Effects of Assets, Performance, Settings, and Ownership on Hospital Closure
content: Background. Differences between for-profit and nonprofit hospitals in finances, staffing, and charity care are well documented, as are size, rural location, and financial position as predictors of hospital closure. It is not known whether ownership carries information about closure beyond measured assets, performance, and settings, or whether ownership, rurality, and performance act independently or jointly on closure risk. Aims. Aim 1 was to test whether ownership is associated with closure beyond measured assets, performance, and settings; Aim 2 was to test whether ownership, rurality, and performance are interdependent correlates of closure that need to be monitored jointly. Methods. We analyzed Medicare cost reports for US short-term acute care and critical access hospitals, fiscal years 2011–2023. Baseline characteristics (2011–2013) were compared by ownership. Discrete-time logistic models (4,833 hospitals, 45,535 hospital-years, 330 closures; observation years 2011–2020) estimated the odds of closure in the following year, with year fixed effects, hospital-clustered standard errors, and sequential adjustment. For-profit versus nonprofit was the primary comparison; government hospitals were examined separately. We tested ownership interactions with rurality, critical access status, size, region, and financial indicators. Results. For-profit hospitals reported higher total margins than nonprofits (median 5.3% versus 4.0%) but fewer days cash on hand (0.6 versus 24.0), fewer staff per bed, and less charity care (1.2% versus 2.3% of costs). Regarding Aim 1, ownership remained associated with closure beyond measured assets, performance, and settings: the for-profit versus nonprofit odds ratio for closure was 3.27 (2.58–4.14) unadjusted and 2.25 (1.69–3.01) fully adjusted; adjustment for financial position did not attenuate it. Government hospitals did not differ from nonprofits (fully adjusted OR 1.19 (0.84–1.68)). Regarding Aim 2, the associations were interdependent. The for-profit association was stronger in rural hospitals (ratio of odds ratios 2.16, 95% CI 1.24–3.76; p=0.006) and critical access hospitals (3.87, 1.70–8.80; p=0.001; 28 closures), but not by size or region. Days cash was associated with lower closure odds in government hospitals (odds ratio per 30 days 0.76 (0.63–0.93)) but not in nonprofit (0.93 (0.83–1.04)) or for-profit hospitals (1.09 (0.99–1.20); interaction p=0.002); operating margin did not differ by ownership (p=0.89). Overall, ownership, rurality, and performance were interdependent rather than independent: ownership differences in resources varied by setting, the interaction terms jointly differed from zero (p = 0.006), and predicted annual closure risk ranged from 2.9 to 14.0 per 1,000 hospital-years across combinations of ownership, rurality, and performance, highest in for-profit hospitals; the associations of operating margin and days cash with closure did not differ detectably between rural and urban hospitals. Conclusions. Closure risk reflects the joint configuration of ownership, rurality, and performance rather than any one alone: ownership identifies closure risk that measured assets, performance, and settings do not capture, chiefly in rural and critical access hospitals, and facility-level liquidity signals closure differently by ownership. These factors should be monitored jointly, and monitoring should not apply a single financial threshold across ownership types.
